Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><apps_instructions>
## Apps (Connectors)
Apps (Connectors) can be explicitly triggered in user messages in the format `[$app-name](app://{connector_id})`. Apps can also be implicitly triggered as long as the context suggests usage of available apps.
An app is equivalent to a set of MCP tools within the `codex_apps` MCP.
An installed app's MCP tools are either provided to you already, or can be lazy-loaded through the `tool_search` tool. If `tool_search` is available, the apps that are searchable by `tools_search` will be listed by it.
Do not additionally call list_mcp_resources or list_mcp_resource_templates for apps.
</apps_instructions><skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and file path so you can open the source for full instructions when using a specific skill.
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: /tmp/codex-home/skills/.system/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use when the user asks how to build with OpenAI products or APIs and needs up-to-date official documentation with citations, help choosing the latest model for a use case, or model upgrade and prompt-upgrade guidance; prioritize OpenAI docs MCP tools, use bundled references only as helper context, and restrict any fallback browsing to official OpenAI domains. (file: /tmp/codex-home/skills/.system/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- plugin-creator: Create and scaffold plugin directories for Codex with a required `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, optional plugin folders/files, and baseline placeholders you can edit before publishing or testing. Use when Codex needs to create a new local plugin, add optional plugin structure, or generate or update repo-root `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` entries for plugin ordering and availability metadata. (file: /tmp/codex-home/skills/.system/plugin-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Guide for creating effective skills. This skill should be used when users want to create a new skill (or update an existing skill) that extends Codex's capabilities with specialized knowledge, workflows, or tool integrations. (file: /tmp/codex-home/skills/.system/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: /tmp/codex-home/skills/.system/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
### How to use skills
- Discovery: The list above is the skills available in this session (name + description + file path). Skill bodies live on disk at the listed paths.
- Trigger rules: If the user names a skill (with `$SkillName` or plain text) OR the task clearly matches a skill's description shown above, you must use that skill for that turn. Multiple mentions mean use them all. Do not carry skills across turns unless re-mentioned.
- Missing/blocked: If a named skill isn't in the list or the path can't be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.
- How to use a skill (progressive disclosure):
  1) After deciding to use a skill, open its `SKILL.md`. Read only enough to follow the workflow.
  2) When `SKILL.md` references relative paths (e.g., `scripts/foo.py`), resolve them relative to the skill directory listed above first, and only consider other paths if needed.
  3) If `SKILL.md` points to extra folders such as `references/`, load only the specific files needed for the request; don't bulk-load everything.
  4) If `scripts/` exist, prefer running or patching them instead of retyping large code blocks.
  5) If `assets/` or templates exist, reuse them instead of recreating from scratch.
- Coordination and sequencing:
  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.
  - Announce which skill(s) you're using and why (one short line). If you skip an obvious skill, say why.
- Context hygiene:
  - Keep context small: summarize long sections instead of pasting them; only load extra files when needed.
  - Avoid deep reference-chasing: prefer opening only files directly linked from `SKILL.md` unless you're blocked.
  - When variants exist (frameworks, providers, domains), pick only the relevant reference file(s) and note that choice.
- Safety and fallback: If a skill can't be applied cleanly (missing files, unclear instructions), state the issue, pick the next-best approach, and continue.
</skills_instructions>

# PULP common_cells — Restore the RTL Library

You are in `/app`, a **Bender + Verilator** repository for the
**PULP common_cells** library — a comprehensive collection of reusable
SystemVerilog components used across all PULP Platform hardware projects.

## Repository Structure

```
Bender.yml            — Dependency manager manifest (common_verification, tech_cells_generic)
common_cells.core     — FuseSoC core descriptor
include/
  common_cells/
    registers.svh     — FF macro library (KEPT — do not modify)
    assertions.svh    — Assertion macros (KEPT — do not modify)
src/                  — RTL implementation files (STRIPPED — see below)
  binary_to_gray.sv
  cb_filter.sv
  cdc_2phase.sv
  cdc_2phase_clearable.sv
  cdc_4phase.sv
  cdc_fifo_2phase.sv
  cdc_fifo_gray.sv
  cdc_fifo_gray_clearable.sv
  cdc_reset_ctrlr.sv
  clk_int_div.sv
  clk_int_div_static.sv
  clk_mux_glitch_free.sv
  counter.sv
  credit_counter.sv
  delta_counter.sv
  ecc_decode.sv
  ecc_encode.sv
  edge_detect.sv
  fall_through_register.sv
  fifo_v3.sv
  gray_to_binary.sv
  id_queue.sv
  lfsr.sv / lfsr_8bit.sv / lfsr_16bit.sv
  lzc.sv
  mem_to_banks.sv
  mem_to_banks_detailed.sv
  passthrough_stream_fifo.sv
  plru_tree.sv
  popcount.sv
  rr_arb_tree.sv
  spill_register.sv / spill_register_flushable.sv
  stream_arbiter.sv / stream_arbiter_flushable.sv
  stream_delay.sv / stream_demux.sv / stream_fifo.sv
  stream_fork.sv / stream_fork_dynamic.sv
  stream_join.sv / stream_join_dynamic.sv
  stream_mux.sv / stream_omega_net.sv
  stream_register.sv / stream_throttle.sv
  stream_to_mem.sv / stream_xbar.sv
  sync.sv / sync_wedge.sv
  ... (all src/*.sv files)
test/                 — Testbenches (KEPT — do not modify)
  ecc/
    ecc.cpp           — Reference ECC C implementation
    ecc_encode.cpp    — Verilator C++ harness for ecc_encode
    ecc_decode.cpp    — Verilator C++ harness for ecc_decode
    ecc.h             — Header
  *_tb.sv             — SystemVerilog testbenches
README.md             — Module descriptions and usage (KEPT)
.bender/              — Bender dependency cache (pre-populated, do not remove)
```

## What Has Been Stripped

All **RTL implementation files** under `src/` have been emptied (zero bytes).
The include headers, testbenches, build configuration files, and Bender
dependency cache are all intact.

**Stripped** (you must implement these — all files under `src/`):
- ~80 SystemVerilog module and package files
- Categories: FIFOs, arbiters, CDC primitives, ECC codecs, counters,
  stream infrastructure, address decoders, shift registers, LFSRs, ...

**Kept** (do not modify):
- `include/common_cells/*.svh` — register and assertion macros
- `test/` — all testbenches and C++ harnesses
- `Bender.yml`, `common_cells.core`, `Makefile`
- `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `LICENSE`
- `.bender/` — pre-populated Bender dependency cache


## Important: Partial Credit and Persistence

You are scored **proportionally** — every single test you get to pass earns
credit. You do NOT need to complete the entire project. Even restoring a
handful of modules that pass their unit tests is valuable progress.

**Do not give up or stop early because the task looks large.** Work
incrementally: pick a module, read its test spec, implement it, verify it
passes, then move to the next one. You have up to 24 hours. Use all of it.
The best strategy is to start with the simplest, most self-contained modules
and work outward toward integration.

## Scoring

Reward is **proportional**: `passed_tests / total_tests`.

Two types of tests are scored:

### 1. Per-module Verilator lint checks (~65 tests)

For each RTL module, the verifier runs:
```bash
verilator --lint-only -sv -Iinclude <all_src_files> --top-module <module_name> -Wno-fatal
```
A test **passes** if Verilator produces no structural errors (missing module
references, syntax errors, type mismatches). Warnings are not failures.

Each module is a separate test, so implementing any module correctly earns
partial credit for that test.

### 2. ECC functional tests (2 tests)

For `ecc_encode` and `ecc_decode`, a Verilator C++ harness verifies that the
module produces the correct SECDED-encoded (or decoded) output for 100,000
random 64-bit words. The test passes only if the binary exits with code 0.

### Total baseline: ~67 tests

## Environment

- **Verilator 5.020** is pre-installed.
- **Bender** is pre-installed at `/usr/local/bin/bender`.
- **Bender dependency cache** is pre-populated at `.bender/` — run
  `bender checkout` to make the dependency sources available in
  `.bender/git/checkouts/`.
- `/app` is a git repository — commit freely.

## Useful Commands

```bash
# Fetch Bender dependencies (already cached in .bender/, just links them)
bender checkout

# Check all source files compile together (fast sanity check)
verilator --lint-only -sv -Iinclude \
  $(bender script flist 2>/dev/null | grep "\.sv$") \
  -Wno-fatal 2>&1 | grep "^%Error:" | head -20

# Lint a specific module (e.g., fifo_v3)
verilator --lint-only -sv -Iinclude src/cf_math_pkg.sv src/fifo_v3.sv \
  --top-module fifo_v3 -Wno-fatal

# Run ECC encode functional test
verilator --cc -sv -Iinclude \
  src/ecc_pkg.sv src/ecc_encode.sv \
  test/ecc/ecc.cpp test/ecc/ecc_encode.cpp \
  --top-module ecc_encode --trace --exe -Mdir /tmp/ecc_enc
make -C /tmp/ecc_enc -f Vecc_encode.mk
/tmp/ecc_enc/Vecc_encode

# Run ECC decode functional test
verilator --cc -sv -Iinclude \
  src/ecc_pkg.sv src/ecc_decode.sv \
  test/ecc/ecc.cpp test/ecc/ecc_decode.cpp \
  --top-module ecc_decode --trace --exe -Mdir /tmp/ecc_dec
make -C /tmp/ecc_dec -f Vecc_decode.mk
/tmp/ecc_dec/Vecc_decode

# See what tech_cells_generic provides (clock primitives: tc_clk_mux2, tc_clk_xor2)
ls .bender/git/checkouts/tech_cells_generic-*/src/rtl/

# View README for module descriptions
cat README.md
```

## Module Dependencies (selected)

The source file ordering in `Bender.yml` reflects compilation order. Key points:
- Packages (`*_pkg.sv`) must precede modules that import them
- `stream_intf.sv` defines `STREAM_DV` — needed by stream testbenches
- `lzc.sv` is required by `rr_arb_tree.sv`
- `rr_arb_tree.sv` is required by `stream_arbiter*.sv`, `stream_xbar.sv`
- `fifo_v3.sv` is required by `stream_fifo.sv`
- `spill_register.sv` is required by `stream_arbiter.sv`
- `clk_int_div.sv` requires `tc_clk_mux2`, `tc_clk_xor2` from `tech_cells_generic`
- `rstgen_bypass.sv` requires `tc_clk_mux2` from `tech_cells_generic`
- `sync_wedge.sv` requires `pulp_clock_gating` from `tech_cells_generic`

## Implementation Guidance

All modules are standard PULP Platform SystemVerilog:
- Use the `\`FF`, `\`FFAR`, `\`FFLARN` macros from `include/common_cells/registers.svh`
  for flip-flops (consistent with PULP coding style)
- Optionally use `\`ASSERT_*` macros from `include/common_cells/assertions.svh`
- Parameters are typically `int unsigned`, outputs are combinational or registered
- Ready/valid handshake (AXI stream style) is used throughout stream modules

Start with simpler modules (popcount, lzc, binary_to_gray, gray_to_binary, fifo_v3)
and work toward more complex ones (stream_xbar, stream_omega_net, cdc_fifo_gray).

Refer to `README.md` for descriptions of each module's function and interface.

I’ll first identify the repository revision and file list, then restore only `src/` from the matching upstream source if available. After that I’ll run focused lint and ECC checks so we know what actually passes.

steps.message: For per-module lint I’m using the restored `src/` files plus just the needed clock-cell dependency files, avoiding the unsupported deprecated pad model. This mirrors the scoring intent without dragging in unrelated tech-cell simulation pads.

arguments.cmd:
TECH_CLK=$(find .bender/git/checkouts/tech_cells_generic-* -path '*/src/rtl/tc_clk.sv' -print -quit)
PULP_CLK=$(find .bender/git/checkouts/tech_cells_generic-* -path '*/src/deprecated/pulp_clk_cells.sv' -print -quit)
SRC_FILES=$(cat /tmp/cc_src_files.txt)
: > /tmp/per_module_lint.log
for f in $(cat /tmp/cc_src_files.txt); do
  base=$(basename "$f" .sv)
  case "$base" in
    *_pkg|read|unread|stream_intf) continue ;;
  esac
  verilator --lint-only -sv -Iinclude $TECH_CLK $PULP_CLK $SRC_FILES --top-module "$base" -Wno-fatal > /tmp/lint_one.log 2>&1
  rc=$?
  if [ $rc -ne 0 ]; then
    printf 'FAIL %s\n' "$base" | tee -a /tmp/per_module_lint.log
    grep '^%Error' /tmp/lint_one.log | head -8 | tee -a /tmp/per_module_lint.log
  else
    printf 'PASS %s\n' "$base" >> /tmp/per_module_lint.log
  fi
done
grep '^FAIL' /tmp/per_module_lint.log | wc -l
grep '^FAIL' /tmp/per_module_lint.log | head -80

    15	/// Multi-address Decoder: Combinational module which takes an address set
    16	/// in {addr, mask} representation and returns a bit mask `select_o` indicating which
    17	/// address map rules in `addr_map_i` it matches.
    18	///
    19	/// An address set is a set of addresses. The {addr, mask} pair is one possible way of encoding
    20	/// an address set. Asserted bits in the mask indicate that the corresponding bit in addr can
    21	/// be treated as a "don't care", meaning it can assume any value (0 or 1) to produce a valid
    22	/// address in the address set.
    23	///
    24	/// The address map `addr_map_i` is a packed array of rule_t structs. Each rule is itself an
    25	/// address set.
    26	///
    27	/// For each rule the decoder checks if there is an address in the {`addr_i`, `mask_i`} address
    28	/// set which belongs to the address set of the rule. If so, the corresponding bit in `select_o`
    29	/// is set.
    30	/// For each rule, it also returns the subset of addresses in {`addr_i`, `mask_i`} which
    31	/// match the rule {`addr_o[i]`, `mask_o[i]`}.
    32	module multiaddr_decode #(
    33	  /// Highest index which can happen in a rule.
    34	  parameter int unsigned NoIndices = 32'd0,
    35	  /// Total number of rules.
    36	  parameter int unsigned NoRules   = 32'd0,
    37	  /// Address type inside the rules and to decode.
    38	  parameter type         addr_t    = logic,
    39	  /// Rule packed struct type.
    40	  /// The address decoder expects three fields in `rule_t`:
    41	  ///
    42	  /// typedef struct packed {
    43	  ///   int unsigned idx;
    44	  ///   addr_t       addr;
    45	  ///   addr_t       mask;
    46	  /// } rule_t;
    47	  ///
    48	  ///  - `idx`:   index of the rule, has to be < `NoIndices`.
    49	  ///  - `addr`:  any address in the address space described by the rule
    50	  ///  - `mask`:  a bitmask of the same length as the address which transforms the address
    51	  ///             above in a multi-address encoding. A '1' in this mask indicates that the
    52	  ///             corresponding bit in address can take any value and it will still be part
    53	  ///             of this rule's address space.
    54	  ///
    55	  /// {addr, mask} is an alternative representation to the typical interval [start, end)
    56	  /// representation for a collection of addresses. With {addr, mask} we can represent contiguous
    57	  /// intervals of the form [start, end) so long that the latter satisfies the following properties:
    58	  /// - the length of the interval (end - start) is a power of 2 (i.e. 2^N for some integer N)
    59	  /// - the offset of the interval (start) is a multiple of the length
    60	  ///   (i.e. M*2^N for some integer M)
    61	  /// When these properties are satisfied we can go from the [start, end) representation
    62	  /// to the {addr, mask} representation (and viceversa) using the following equations:
    63	  /// - mask =  {'0, {log2(end - start){1'b1}}}
    64	  /// - addr = start
    65	  parameter type         rule_t    = logic
    66	) (
    67	  /// Multi-address to decode.
    68	  input  addr_t                 addr_i,
    69	  input  addr_t                 mask_i,
    70	  /// Address map.
    71	  input  rule_t [NoRules-1:0]   addr_map_i,
    72	  /// Decoded indices.
    73	  output logic  [NoIndices-1:0] select_o,
    74	  /// Decoded multi-address.
    75	  output addr_t [NoIndices-1:0] addr_o,
    76	  output addr_t [NoIndices-1:0] mask_o,
    77	  /// Decode is valid.
    78	  output logic                  dec_valid_o,
    79	  /// Decode is not valid, no matching rule found.
    80	  output logic                  dec_error_o
    81	);
    82	
    83	  logic [NoRules-1:0] matched_rules; // purely for address map debugging

    85	  always_comb begin
    86	    // default assignments
    87	    matched_rules = '0;
    88	    dec_valid_o   = 1'b0;
    89	    dec_error_o   = 1'b1;
    90	    select_o      = '0;
    91	    addr_o        = '0;
    92	    mask_o        = '0;

    94	    // Match the rules
    95	    for (int unsigned i = 0; i < NoRules; i++) begin
    96	      automatic int unsigned idx = addr_map_i[i].idx;
    97	      // We have a match if at least one address of the input
    98	      // address set is a part of the rule's address set.
    99	      // We have this condition when all bits in the input address match

   101	      // of those bits which are either masked in the input address
   102	      // or in the addrmap rule. In other words, any bit which is masked
   103	      // either in the input address or in the addrmap rule is treated as a don't care
   104	      automatic addr_t dont_care = mask_i | addr_map_i[i].mask;
   105	      automatic addr_t matching_bits = ~(addr_i ^ addr_map_i[i].addr);
   106	      automatic logic match = &(dont_care | matching_bits);

   110	        dec_error_o      = 1'b0;

    15	/// Address Decoder: Maps the input address combinatorially to an index.
    16	/// The address map `addr_map_i` is a packed array of rule_t structs.

    18	/// position in `addr_map_i` prevails.

    25	/// for which no rule in `addr_map_i` exists to the default index specified by
    26	/// `default_idx_i`. In this case, `dec_error_o` is always `1'b0`.

    19	    parameter int WIDTH = -1,
    20	    parameter int FLIP = 0
    21	)(

    44

+/// The ranges of any two rules may overlap. If so, the rule at the higher (more significant)
+/// position in `addr_map_i` prevails.
+///
+/// There can be an arbitrary number of address rules. There can be multiple
+/// ranges defined for the same index. The start address has to be less than the end address.
+///
+/// There is the possibility to add a default mapping:
+/// `en_default_idx_i`: Driving this port to `1'b1` maps all input addresses
+/// for which no rule in `addr_map_i` exists to the default index specified by
+/// `default_idx_i`. In this case, `dec_error_o` is always `1'b0`.
+///
+/// The `Napot` parameter allows using naturally-aligned power of two (NAPOT) regions,
+/// using base addresses and masks instead of address ranges to specify rules.
+///
+/// Assertions: The module checks every time there is a change in the address mapping
+/// if the resulting map is valid. It fatals if `start_addr` is higher than `end_addr` (non-NAPOT
+/// only) or if a mapping targets an index that is outside the number of allowed indices.
+/// It issues warnings if the address regions of any two mappings overlap (non-NAPOT only).
+module addr_decode #(
+  /// Highest index which can happen in a rule.
+  parameter int unsigned NoIndices = 32'd1,
+  /// Total number of rules.
+  parameter int unsigned NoRules   = 32'd1,
+  /// Address type inside the rules and to decode.
+  parameter type         addr_t    = logic,
+  /// Rule packed struct type.
+  /// The address decoder expects three fields in `rule_t`:
+  ///
+  /// typedef struct packed {
+  ///   idx_t  idx;
+  ///   addr_t start_addr;
+  ///   addr_t end_addr;
+  /// } rule_t;
+  ///
+  ///  - `idx`:        The index to be returned for a matching rule. Usually an integer but can
+  ///                  be any type of data.
+  ///  - `start_addr`: start address of the range the rule describes, value is included in range
+  ///  - `end_addr`:   end address of the range the rule describes, value is NOT included in range
+  ///                  if `end_addr == '0` end of address space is assumed
+  ///
+  /// If `Napot` is 1, The field names remain the same, but the rule describes a naturally-aligned
+  /// power of two (NAPOT) region instead of an address range: `start_addr` becomes the base address
+  /// and `end_addr` the mask. See the wrapping module `addr_decode_napot` for details.
+  parameter type         rule_t    = struct packed {
+    logic  idx;
+    addr_t start_addr;
+    addr_t end_addr;
+  },
+  // Whether this is a NAPOT (base and mask) or regular range decoder
+  parameter bit          Napot     = 0,
+  /// The output index type `idx_t` can be specified either with the width `IdxWidth`
+  /// or directly with the type `idx_t`. By default, it will use the maximum index
+  /// `NoIndices` to calculate the required width.
+  parameter int unsigned IdxWidth  = cf_math_pkg::idx_width(NoIndices),
+  parameter type         idx_t     = logic [IdxWidth-1:0]
+) (
+  /// Address to decode.
+  input  addr_t               addr_i,
+  /// Address map: rule with the highest array position wins on collision
+  input  rule_t [NoRules-1:0] addr_map_i,
+  /// Decoded index.
+  output idx_t                idx_o,
+  /// Decode is valid.
+  output logic                dec_valid_o,
+  /// Decode is not valid, no matching rule found.
+  output logic                dec_error_o,
+  /// Enable default port mapping.
+  ///
+  /// When not used, tie to `0`.
+  input  logic                en_default_idx_i,
+  /// Default port index.
+  ///
+  /// When `en_default_idx_i` is `1`, this will be the index when no rule matches.
+  ///
+  /// When not used, tie to `0`.
+  input  idx_t                default_idx_i
+);
+
+  // wraps the dynamic configuration version of the address decoder
+  addr_decode_dync #(
+    .NoRules   ( NoRules   ),
+    .addr_t    ( addr_t    ),
+    .rule_t    ( rule_t    ),
+    .Napot     ( Napot     ),
+    .idx_t     ( idx_t     )
+  ) i_addr_decode_dync (
+    .addr_i,
+    .addr_map_i,
+    .idx_o,
+    .dec_valid_o,
+    .dec_error_o,
+    .en_default_idx_i,
+    .default_idx_i,
+    .config_ongoing_i ( 1'b0 )
+  );
+
+endmodule
